Hi Avichal Dwivedi,

Your team Cue has completed web check-in. You’re ready to build!

As team leader, you receive the setup and credits instructions for your team. Credits are allocated once per team, not per member.

## Join the neatHack Discord

Join our Discord for event announcements, help with setup and credits, and support from organisers and mentors.

[https://neatlogs.com/discord](https://neatlogs.com/discord)

## 1. Build with neatlogs — free throughout the hackathon

All neatlogs paid plans are available to you for free for the duration of neatHack. We believe no good idea should be held back by a paywall.

Sign up at [https://app.neatlogs.com](https://app.neatlogs.com) and create your project.

Start with our step-by-step setup guide, with screenshots, a ready-to-use coding-agent prompt, and troubleshooting: [https://neatlogs.com/hackathon/neatlogs-setup-guide.html](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon/neatlogs-setup-guide.html)

For framework-specific instructions, see [https://docs.neatlogs.com.](https://docs.neatlogs.com)

Run your agent and verify that its traces appear in the dashboard. Use those traces to investigate failures and verify your fixes.

## 2. Set up Entire

Follow the Entire guide for neatHack: [https://hack.entire.io/neathacks-2026/](https://hack.entire.io/neathacks-2026/)

Connect your GitHub repository, install the CLI, and capture your first checkpoint.

Explore Trails and optional Graph/Brain features. Include an accessible checkpoint link and ID in your submission.

## 3. Access [cfo.ai](http://cfo.ai/) paid plans for free

Use the dedicated neatHack signup link to access any [cfo.ai](http://cfo.ai/) paid plan for free: [https://cfo.ai/neathacks](https://cfo.ai/neathacks)

A card is required during signup. Immediately after signing up, cancel your subscription in Settings → Billing. You won’t be billed if you cancel immediately.

The neatHack team will provide your [cfo.ai](http://cfo.ai/) credits directly.

Use [cfo.ai](http://cfo.ai/) to plan your agent’s pricing, costs, revenue, and runway. Include the resulting business plan in your submission.

## 4. Claim your Crustdata credits

Get 5,000 Crustdata credits to build with company and people data.

Use promo code: NEATLOGS-OCT2026

Open [https://app.crustdata.com](https://app.crustdata.com) and select “Have a promo code?” below Continue. Add the code before signing up with your email. Use email signup, not “Continue with Google”, so the code can be applied. Already have an account, or need help? Contact the neatHack organisers at [https://neatlogs.com/discord.](https://neatlogs.com/discord)

API documentation: [https://www.crustdata.com/api-documentation](https://www.crustdata.com/api-documentation)

## Before you build

Every project must use neatlogs, Entire, and [cfo.ai](http://cfo.ai/). Keep evidence of all three for your submission and demo.

Hackathon guide: [https://neatlogs.com/hackathon](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon)

Build-log skill: [https://neatlogs.com/hackathon/skill](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon/skill)

View your team: [https://neatlogs.com/hackathon/check-in](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon/check-in)

Get help on Discord: [https://neatlogs.com/discord](https://neatlogs.com/discord)

See you at neatHack!

The neatlogs team

content.text:
**Yes—Cue fits this track well. I’d keep the core idea.** Its customer report → investigation → code change → independent tests → human approval → verified resolution workflow directly matches what they’re asking for.

After inspecting the code and verification records, I’d prioritize these changes:

1. **Complete the required sponsor integrations.** I couldn’t find neatlogs instrumentation, accessible Entire checkpoint evidence, or a cfo.ai business plan in the checked-in project. These are mandatory, and effective sponsor use carries **25% of the score**. [Official criteria](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon)

2. **Make one complete workflow the main demo.** Show a customer reporting a Bloom problem, Cue investigating and producing a tested fix, then the approval and verified outcome. Explain where humans approve consequential actions.

3. **Show failure and recovery.** Capture a failed run and an improved run in neatlogs, with the same task and a measurable difference. That demonstrates why Cue is useful beyond its interface.

4. **Prepare a public submission repository.** I verified that `cue-b2c` is currently private; they require public code and a demo of three minutes or less. [Submission requirements](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon)

Growth can be a supporting example. Its recorded journey proves a controlled activation, but organic acquisition remains unproven—keep the sample metrics clearly labelled. [Verification report](/Users/avichaldwivedi/dev/Cue/cue-demo/docs/REDACTED.md:23)

**My recommendation: finish the sponsor evidence and prove one fresh end-to-end run before expanding Cue further.**

+# Cue business plan — neatHack 2026
+
+Cue helps small consumer-app teams turn customer reports into investigated,
+reviewed, and verified product changes. The first customer is a founder or a
+small product team maintaining one app and receiving repeated support reports.
+Bloom is our controlled demonstration app, not a paying customer.
+
+## Offer and pricing hypothesis
+
+Test a $99/month plan for one app: 50 support conversations and five scoped
+coding investigations, with human approval before publishing or releasing.
+This is a proposed pilot price, not a launched plan or willingness-to-pay result.
+Start with three to five design partners. Retain manual review for uncertain
+grouping and limit coding to a connected, trusted repository and approved paths.
+
+## Cost model
+
+All dollar amounts below are planning allowances, not measured provider bills.
+Assume $0.02 per support conversation, $3 per coding investigation, $3 variable
+infrastructure per customer, and $75/month fixed hosting/observability/tools.
+Variable cost is therefore $19/customer/month. Cost of a coding investigation
+is the biggest unmeasured expense; capture real usage before selling a quota.
+
+| Paying customers | Revenue/month | Cost/month | Contribution/month | Margin |
+|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
+| 0 | $0 | $75 | -$75 | — |
+| 1 | $99 | $94 | $5 | 5.1% |
+| 5 | $495 | $170 | $325 | 65.7% |
+| 20 | $1,980 | $455 | $1,525 | 77.0% |
+
+Formula: revenue = customers × 99; cost = 75 + customers × 19.
+Founder salary, taxes, payment fees, sales effort, and refunds are excluded;
+these are contribution margins, not net profit. Hackathon credits are excluded
+from steady-state economics. With a hypothetical $1,000 cash budget and zero
+revenue, infrastructure-only runway is 13.3 months at $75/month. Cash and funding
+have not been supplied, so this is a scenario rather than actual runway.
+
+Stress case: at $12 per investigation, variable cost becomes $64/customer.
+At 20 customers, contribution drops to $625/month and margin to 31.6%.
+Fallback: charge expensive coding runs separately, reduce the included quota,
+or provide investigation-only workflows until costs are predictable.
+
+## Smallest falsifiable pilot
+
+Recruit three founders with a trusted app repository. Over one week, compare
+ten eligible support reports per founder with their current manual workflow.
+Match report complexity and record elapsed human work, coding/provider cost,
+independent acceptance checks, rejected suggestions, and required edits.
+Keep a separate set of unseen reports for final assessment.
+
+Success: at least 30% less human work on eligible reports, zero cross-app data
+exposure or unsupported release claims, independent checks passing before
+resolution, and at least two founders agreeing to the $99 paid pilot.
+Stop automatic grouping on any false merge. Stop autonomous implementation on
+any protected-file change or approval bypass. Pivot to support investigation
+and draft preparation if median human savings are below 20%, or if fewer than
+two founders want to pay. Add complexity only after this baseline succeeds.
+
+## Current evidence and limits
+
+The inspected application retains a real scoped Codex investigation, protected
+tests, a reviewed commit, and deployed acceptance evidence. A fresh replay of
+the upload fixture produces three failed acceptance checks before the limit
+fix and eight passing HTTP checks afterward. This replay applies the existing
+one-line correction in a temporary copy; it is not a new autonomous coding run.
+Fresh Gemini support, classification, specification, and Growth calls have
+neatlogs traces. Their controlled drafts were not sent to customers.
+
+Growth has a previously verified controlled publication-to-Bloom activation
+journey. Organic acquisition, retention, paid customers, and revenue are
+unmeasured. Generic arbitrary-repository bug fixing and unattended releases
+are outside the demonstrated scope.
+

+trial/card step and immediately canceling the subscription, as instructed in
+the event email. This document is the prepared model input. It must not be

readme='''# Cue · neatHack 2026

Cue helps consumer-app teams turn customer feedback into investigated, reviewed and independently verified product changes. Bloom is the reference photo-journal app.

- [Cue](https://cue.latchgrid.in) · [operator workspace](https://cue.latchgrid.in/cue#/home) (sign-in and team membership required)
- [Bloom customer app](https://bloom-with-cue.vercel.app)
- [Business plan](docs/neathack-business-plan.md) · [Demo script](docs/neathack-demo-script.md) · [Submission evidence](docs/neathack-submission.md)

## What works

Support reports are saved, classified and linked to issues. Cue can run a scoped Codex investigation against its Bloom fixture, keep independent tests outside the editable surface, and require human approval of the exact patch before release. App-bound feature repositories have a separate trusted execution path. Arbitrary repositories and arbitrary bug deployment are outside this demo's supported scope.

The retained upload run has a real coding session, independently checked patch and approved release. Fresh neatlogs evidence includes actual Gemini support/triage/specification/Growth calls and a temporary-copy replay of the upload regression. The replay applies the known correction; it is not a new autonomous coding run. Growth activation evidence is controlled; no organic acquisition or paying customers are claimed.

## Run locally

> “Bloom promises uploads up to 5 MB, but a 3 MB photo fails. Cue investigates, writes a fix, tests it, and asks for approval before release.”

Use this sequence—the existing **2:29 video** follows it:

| Time | What to show and explain |
|---|---|
| **0:00–0:18** | Cue’s workflow: customer report → investigation → coding → testing → human approval. |
| **0:18–1:01** | The actual Codex patch correcting the 2 MB server limit, eight independent checks, and approval of the exact commit. |
| **1:01–1:23** | **neatlogs:** three failing checks before the correction, eight passing afterward. Explain how traces help verify improvement. |
| **1:23–1:46** | An actual Gemini trace showing model inputs, output and token usage. |
| **1:46–2:04** | **Entire:** open the checkpoint so judges can inspect the coding context and associated commit. |
| **2:04–2:29** | **cfo.ai:** show proposed $99/month pricing and how higher coding costs change the economics. Label these as planning assumptions. |

Be explicit that the patch is from a retained actual run and the comparison is a **known-fix replay**. The production bug is already fixed. Crustdata can stay out of this demo until Cue actually uses it.

*** Add File: /Users/avichaldwivedi/dev/Cue/cue-demo/docs/crustdata-customer-research.md
+# Crustdata customer research for Cue
+
+Open **Growth → Cue customers** in the signed-in [Cue workspace](https://cue.latchgrid.in/cue#/growth/prospects).
+Describe a company cohort, click **Find companies**, then review the returned
+facts and use **Shortlist**, **Dismiss**, or **Return to review**. These are
+potential buyers of Cue, separate from Bloom's explicit-request Growth flow.
+
+## Implementation
+
+The authenticated Next.js route derives the actor from the saved workspace
+membership. Owner and Product members can search/review; other signed-in team
+members can read. Same-origin checks protect writes. Convex keeps the key in a
+server environment variable and stores research runs and company facts.
+
+The action reads free account permission/pricing metadata, reserves a bounded
+run, performs [hybrid company search](https://docs.crustdata.com/company-docs/search/introduction)
+with reported headcount 1–50, then requests
+[company enrichment](https://docs.crustdata.com/company-docs/enrichment/introduction)
+by the exact returned company IDs. Requested fields are company name, domain,
+description, headcount and country. Person/contact endpoints are unused.
+Provider-response extras are discarded before saving; neatlogs records
+request metadata and usage, rather than the raw response.
+
+Each search returns at most five companies, has a 15-credit reservation ceiling,
+and allows at most five reserved searches per UTC day. Reservations are atomic;
+duplicate request keys reuse the existing run, failures retain their reservation,
+and paid provider calls are never automatically retried. Repeated company IDs
+update facts while preserving human shortlist decisions. Missing or ambiguous
+enrichment produces review-only search evidence. The UI displays unavailable
+usage as unknown rather than guessing a dollar conversion.
+
+## Live check on October 11, 2026
+
+The corrected deployed action returned five exact-ID enriched records and
+reported **11.15 credits** across search and enrichment, equal to its reservation.
+The initial filter request failed because Crustdata's inclusive operators are
+`=>` and `=<`; a diagnostic response reported zero credits for that rejection.
+The failed run remains recorded. No company was contacted.
+
+| Company | Crustdata-reported employees | Independent product-site observation |
+|---|---:|---|
+| Reflection | 4 | [Official site](https://www.reflection.app/) describes a journaling app on iOS, Android, macOS and web. |
+| Atoms | 5 | [James Clear's official site](https://jamesclear.com/) links the official Atomic Habits app. |
+| HabitYou | 1 | [Official site](https://habityou.com/) links iOS/Android habit tracking, journaling and planning. |
+| Habit Nest | 8 | [Official site](https://habitnest.com/) describes its mobile app alongside physical journals. |
+| Raz Industries | 1 | No website returned; product identity remains unverified. |
+
+Employee counts are provider-reported observations, not independently confirmed.
+The fit rule is a simple description/category plus team-size baseline. It does
+not establish support pain, current engineering capacity, a decision-maker,
+budget, permission to contact, or willingness to pay. The website checks support
+product identity only. Five records are a smoke test, not acquisition evidence.
+
+## Smallest next validation
+
+Review 20 unseen company records against a manual product-site baseline before
+expanding search. Use the same headcount target and research budget for both
+methods. Success: at least 80% correctly identified consumer-app teams and at
+least 30% less review time, with zero identity mismatches in the shortlist.
+Stop automatic fit labeling on any identity mismatch; pivot to raw company
+facts and manual review if precision is below 80%. Founder conversations and
+a measured paid pilot are separate future work requiring user authorization.
+
+## Configuration and checks
+
+Set `CRUSTDATA_API_KEY` and `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` on the existing Convex deployment
+using `npx convex env set NAME --from-file private-value-file`. Keep key files
+outside tracked source; never use `NEXT_PUBLIC_` for either key. Deploy with
+`npx convex deploy`. The website needs its existing authenticated Convex
+connection and server secret; no Crustdata key is delivered to the browser.
+
+Tests cover request field selection and exact-ID association, partial failure,
+pricing ceilings, atomic reservations and duplicate keys, role/secret checks,
+CSRF, decision preservation, and metadata-only telemetry. Full backend suite:
+319 passing tests across 46 files; lint, typecheck and production build passed.
*** End Patch"));

I’m assuming you mean the **Bloom app** we use to demonstrate Cue. I’ll check its current flow and suggest a stronger demo scenario.

If you mean **Bloom**, I’d keep its foundation and make the customer story more compelling. It already has working photo storage and support connected to Cue.

I’m thinking **a travel-memory journal**: a polished trip timeline, photos and captions, with one clear journey:

1. A user tries to save an important trip photo and encounters a failure.
2. They report it through Bloom’s support.
3. Cue investigates, proposes a fix and runs independent tests.
4. A person approves the change.
5. The user retries successfully—the memory appears in their journal.

That makes Cue’s value visible. We’d use an isolated demo version for the failure, since the existing upload bug is already fixed.

If we replace Bloom entirely, my second choice is a **habit tracker with a broken streak calculation**. The before-and-after would be obvious, but it needs a new tested integration.

**My recommendation: improve Bloom’s experience first.** A quick live walkthrough should establish whether the problem, Cue’s intervention and the successful outcome are immediately understandable before we invest in a replacement.

Okay now how do we connect Cue with our own apps. There should be an easy way to integrate it right. Like does it happen through an api or something like that and also how is Cue connected to the knowledge base of the company so it can have context and shit
I’ll check Cue’s current integration and context paths so I can explain what works today and what we’d need to make setup easy for another app.

Yes—**our own web apps can already connect to Cue through a copy-paste support widget. The company knowledge-base connection still needs to be built.**

For an app today:

1. Open [Cue setup](https://cue.latchgrid.in/setup#widget).
2. Register the app’s name and website domain.
3. Paste the generated script into the app:

```html
<script async
  src="https://cue.latchgrid.in/widget.js"
  data-app="YOUR_REGISTERED_APP_ID">
</script>
```

The widget talks to Cue’s API behind the scenes. It handles support conversations, attachments and replies, with separate visitor sessions. A native mobile app or custom support interface would need a proper SDK or documented API—we haven’t packaged that yet.

For context, there are **three different connections**:

| Connection | What it gives Cue | Today |
|---|---|---|
| App/widget | Customer messages and the page where they need help | Working |
| Company knowledge | Product guides, FAQs, policies and troubleshooting instructions | Missing |
| GitHub repository | Code, repository instructions and tests for engineering work | Working within configured, trusted repository policies |

**Today, Cue gets context from saved conversations, issues, approved specifications, tests and release evidence. Some prompts also contain Bloom-specific instructions.** It doesn’t automatically know a company’s documentation, and connecting GitHub doesn’t automatically make those documents available to the support agent.

I’d make the next improvement a **Knowledge sources** screen. Initially, we should support pasted text and uploaded documents. For each question, Cue would retrieve relevant passages, use them alongside the conversation and cite the source. Missing information should stay unknown. Notion, Google Drive and website syncing can follow once that basic flow works.

The first proof should be connecting another app, adding its product guide and FAQ, then asking questions that require those documents—including one they cannot answer. That would demonstrate Cue adapting beyond Bloom.

Our additional apps can use the current workspace. Before onboarding separate companies, we also need company-level data and connection isolation.

Also should we not like do something so that Cue can get the whole company's context from different sources and stuff like that? Also should we also focus on customer support as well if the person is asking something through the widget or that is a bad idea?

**Yes—company context and customer support should be central to Cue.** They connect naturally: Cue answers product questions, learns where customers struggle, and carries validated problems through to reviewed fixes.

I’d build a shared context layer from selected sources:

- **Product knowledge:** guides, FAQs, pricing and policies.
- **Current product state:** changelogs, known issues and verified releases.
- **Engineering context:** repository instructions, architecture and tests.
- **Customer history:** relevant conversations and previous resolutions.

Each request should retrieve the relevant information with its source, freshness and company/app permissions. Connecting a company shouldn’t mean feeding every document and Slack message into every answer.

The widget should handle different requests differently:

| Customer request | Cue’s response |
|---|---|
| “How do I use this?” | Answer from approved documentation, with a source |
| “Something is broken” | Gather useful details and link or create a bug report |
| “Could you add this?” | Capture the need for Product review |
| Missing information or an account-specific action | Ask a focused question or hand off to a person |

Okay then build the FAQs and context UI, connect it to the widget, and claim the LiteLLM credits as well and also build the whole context and retrieval shit as well. But first i want a plan exactly how will u have the context and retrieval

I’ll map the retrieval flow against Cue’s existing widget and backend, then give you a concrete plan before making changes. I’m using the codebase-design skill to define how sources, permissions, retrieval and answers fit together.

Cue already saves conversations and workflow status, but it has no document retrieval. I’ll keep those as separate kinds of evidence: approved knowledge for product answers, and verified workflow records for claims about fixes or releases. Both will pass through the same permission checks before reaching the model.

I’d build **one knowledge module shared by the widget and Cue’s internal agents**. FAQs, documents and connectors would feed that module, so adding a new source wouldn’t require changing how the widget answers.

Here’s the exact plan.

**1. Add a Knowledge section in Cue**

The UI would offer:

| Input | What the team supplies |
|---|---|
| FAQ | Question, alternative phrasings and approved answer |
| Write/paste | Product details, policies or instructions |
| Upload | TXT, Markdown, text-based PDF and DOCX |
| Website | A specific public documentation page |
| Connector | Selected repository documents; Notion and Drive follow afterward |

Every source gets an application assignment, customer-facing/internal visibility, and **Draft → Preview → Publish** controls. The preview shows what Cue actually extracted. Scanned PDFs would show that OCR is needed rather than silently importing empty content.

A “Test a question” panel would show the answer and the passages used.

**2. Store original sources, versions and searchable passages**

I’ll use the existing Convex backend, with separate records for:

- **Sources:** title, type, workspace, assigned applications, visibility and publication status.
- **Versions:** original file/text, content hash and revision.
- **Chunks:** searchable passages with their source, revision, heading and PDF page number.
- **Answer evidence:** which passages and model produced each reply.

Editing a published document creates a draft revision. Publishing switches the active revision; withdrawing a source immediately makes it ineligible for new answers.

**3. Process each source once**

The ingestion flow would be:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["FAQ / text / document / page"] --> B["Extract and preview"]
    B --> C["Publish approved version"]
    C --> D["Split into passages"]
    D --> E["Keyword index + embeddings"]
    E --> F["Retrieve for each question"]
```

FAQs stay together as complete question-and-answer passages. Longer documents split at headings and paragraphs, targeting roughly **400–600 tokens**, with a small overlap.

I’ll preserve the actual text rather than replacing documents with model-generated summaries. Import jobs will have visible progress, bounded retries and clear failures.

**4. Use keyword and semantic retrieval together**

For each customer question:

1. Validate the widget session and derive its application and workspace on the server.
2. Build a search query from the question and relevant recent conversation.
3. Retrieve up to **10 keyword matches and 10 semantic matches**.
4. Recheck source permissions, publication status and active revision.
5. Merge rankings, remove duplicate passages and select roughly **four passages**, within a context limit.

Keyword search helps with exact product names, error messages and policy terms. Semantic search handles questions phrased differently from the documentation. Convex supports both, so we can keep the indexes in our existing backend. [Text search](https://docs.convex.dev/search/text-search), [vector search](https://docs.convex.dev/search/vector-search)

For embeddings, I propose **`gemini-embedding-001` with 768 dimensions**, using our existing Google backend credentials after verifying access. Embeddings are a separate cost from the LiteLLM allowance. Unchanged passages can reuse their embeddings. [Google embedding documentation](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/embeddings/get-text-embeddings)

**5. Assemble the answer from three kinds of context**

The model receives:

| Context | What it establishes |
|---|---|
| Published customer-facing knowledge | Product instructions, FAQs and policies |
| This visitor’s conversation | Their question and details already supplied |
| Verified Cue workflow records | Actual investigation, approval and release status |

This matters: a document describing a feature cannot prove that a fix was deployed. Workflow records remain the authority for those claims.

Internal documents stay available to authorised staff and engineering agents. They never enter a public widget prompt.

**6. Connect answers and citations to the widget**

Widget replies would display source cards such as **“Upload guide · page 3”**. Uploaded documents would expose approved excerpts through checked routes, rather than handing visitors unrestricted file links.

The reply would be a structured result: **answered, clarification needed, conflicting sources, or handoff needed**. Citation IDs must belong to the retrieved passages. Missing evidence should produce a useful clarification or handoff, without inventing a policy.

An exact match to an approved FAQ can return its answer directly.

**7. Claim LiteLLM and measure model choice**

After this plan, I’ll claim Cue’s team key using your check-in email and keep it server-side. The shared allowance is **$20**. [Claim page](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon/models)

I’ll compare Nova Lite and Claude Haiku against our current Gemini baseline using identical retrieved context. Sonnet will be tested for harder questions. Model selection will follow answer quality, latency and measured cost.

neatlogs will record retrieval choices, model usage and failures, with document contents excluded from routine telemetry.

**8. Build and verify in stages**

The order is **FAQ/text storage and permissions → widget answers → file/page ingestion → hybrid retrieval → model comparison**. All inputs use the same retrieval interface; OAuth connectors can then feed it.

I’ll compare keyword-only retrieval with hybrid retrieval on separate development and held-out questions. The release targets are **at least 90% correct, supported responses**, valid citations, and zero cross-application or internal-document disclosures. Tests will include withdrawn documents, conflicting policies and missing answers.

The core is roughly **8–16 focused hours**, subject to parser and provider access issues. Cue’s wider company self-service still needs its existing workspace migration; this build will explicitly scope the new knowledge within the current pilot.

text(await tools.apply_patch("*** Begin Patch
*** Add File: /Users/avichaldwivedi/dev/Cue/cue-demo/docs/company-knowledge.md
+# Company knowledge in Cue
+
+Open [Knowledge](https://cue.latchgrid.in/knowledge), select your registered application, and add an FAQ, pasted text, a file, a public website page, or a public GitHub document. Support can save drafts; Product and Owner can publish or withdraw them. Customer-facing sources are eligible for widget answers. Internal sources are available only to authorised staff in the agent workspace.
+
+Files supported: TXT, Markdown, text-based PDF and DOCX, up to 10 MB. PDFs are limited to 100 pages. Extracted content is limited to 200,000 characters and 160 passages. Scanned PDFs require OCR before upload. Each website import fetches one public HTTPS page; use **Refresh page draft** to fetch an update. Private Notion, Drive and GitHub OAuth connectors are not part of this release. Upload or paste their approved content instead.
+
+Review the extracted preview, save the draft, then publish. Edits create immutable revisions. Publishing embeds the saved revision in a background workpool, and switches retrieval atomically only when all passages are indexed. The previous published revision remains available during indexing. Failed indexing retains completed embeddings and offers manual retry. Publishing rejects stale editor revisions. Withdrawing immediately makes the source ineligible for new answers and invalidates pending publication work.
+
+## Retrieval and answers
+
+Convex text search and native vector search are filtered by a composite workspace/application/audience key. Google `gemini-embedding-001` produces 768-dimension document and query vectors. Reciprocal rank fusion selects at most four passages, with at most two per source. A query embedding failure uses keyword retrieval. The backend rechecks the current publication, version, workspace, application and visibility after search and atomically before saving a customer answer.
+
+An exact approved FAQ question or alternative uses its published answer without an answer-model call. Other product questions use the selected model with the bounded passages, public conversation history and independently verified workflow facts. Passages are untrusted data. Answered product responses require citations to retrieved passages. Missing information and conflicting policies should produce a clarification or review response. These are model instructions with citation validation, not a mathematical guarantee of factual correctness.
+
+Typed and spoken widget questions share this service. Voice still uses Gemini for transcription and Google Cloud for speech; its consent notice includes the configured answer provider. Customer source cards show the document title, heading or PDF page and the cited excerpt. Private storage URLs and file IDs stay on the server. Historical cards stop displaying excerpts when their source is withdrawn or superseded; the saved conversational answer itself remains part of the case history.
+
+Knowledge receipts retain the used and cited passage IDs, application, workspace, model, retrieval mode and reported answer-model token usage. SDK tracing hides document payload fields; embedding calls are not instrumented with raw document content. Exact FAQ answers do not consume answer-model tokens, but hybrid retrieval can still consume query-embedding usage. Unreported fallback usage is labelled unavailable rather than described as free.
+
+## LiteLLM
+
+The neatHack team key is held in the private Cloud Run runtime secret, never in client code or the repository. The team claim screen confirmed one shared $20 allowance. This is the original allocation, not a live remaining balance. Supported chat models are Nova Lite, Claude Haiku and Claude Sonnet 4.6, with Gemini Flash available for comparison. Provider errors, exhausted allowance and unavailable models produce a controlled review answer; there is no silent retry to a more expensive provider.
+
+Use the Knowledge question tester to see the answer, supporting excerpts, retrieved passages, model, retrieval mode and reported tokens. Advanced controls compare hybrid retrieval with the keyword baseline. Tests do not message customers.
+
+## Evaluation protocol
+
+`tests/fixtures/knowledge-evaluation.json` freezes three development questions and twenty held-out questions before results are inspected. Its synthetic documents cover correct facts, paraphrases, missing information, conflicting policies, unpublished drafts, prompt injection, and canaries in private, other-application and other-workspace documents. They are isolated from registered live applications and withdrawn after execution.
+
+Run with the trusted server environment and a private team key:
+
+```sh
+node --env-file=.env.local --import tsx scripts/evaluate-knowledge.ts
+```
+
+The script compares Gemini Flash, Nova Lite and Haiku with the same corpus and 1,200-token answer cap, plus a matched Haiku keyword baseline. No provider retry or model fallback is allowed. The initial gate is at least 18/20 correct, appropriately supported responses or abstentions and zero canary disclosure. Pattern checks are a bounded regression screen; manually inspect the answer and its evidence before interpreting this as support quality. Twenty synthetic questions cannot establish general customer accuracy. Keep a failed question out of the tuning set and use new development questions to diagnose mechanisms.
+
+The current deployment is the configured single-company pilot. It has strict app and public/internal separation inside that company; it is not yet an independent organisation-onboarding product with per-document user ACLs. No unattended crawling, connector auto-sync, OCR, or full company chat ingestion is claimed.
*** End Patch"));

+The current deployment is the configured single-company pilot. It has strict app and public/internal separation inside that company; it is not yet an independent organisation-onboarding product with per-document user ACLs. No unattended crawling, connector auto-sync, OCR, or full company chat ingestion is claimed.
+
+## October 12 verification and model choice
+
+The first frozen run exposed response-format failures: Nova often copied unquoted keys from a typed schema example, and Haiku sometimes prepended prose because the existing reply policy also requested plain text. Two development questions reproduced both mechanisms. Removing the conflicting plain-text instruction and using a literal valid JSON example made all six development model calls produce cited answers. Rejected responses now retain reported token usage and mark their failure stage in neatlogs. The original run is preserved in [the initial results](evidence/knowledge-evaluation.json).
+
+Twenty fresh questions were frozen after that repair, without further prompt tuning. Exact FAQ matching was disabled to test the actual model path. [Full responses and evidence titles](evidence/knowledge-evaluation-v2.json) are retained.
+
+| Model / retrieval | Passed | Canary disclosures | Median measured latency | Reported answer tokens, total |
+|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
+| Gemini Flash / hybrid | 19/20 | 0 | 3,901 ms | 26,245 |
+| Nova Lite / hybrid | 19/20 | 0 | 2,643 ms | 26,401 |
+| Claude Haiku / hybrid | 19/20 | 0 | 2,943 ms | 28,401 |
+| Claude Haiku / keyword | 19/20 | 0 | 1,794 ms | 24,128 |
+
+Haiku remains the widget default: its remaining failure was a controlled refusal to answer, while Gemini incorrectly said a one-word caption satisfied a two-word all-terms query, and Nova chose a 14-day cancellation deadline despite a conflicting 30-day source. Haiku also has a successful conflict response. The keyword baseline matched hybrid on this small corpus; these results do not establish a quality advantage for semantic retrieval. Model comparisons were concurrent and the keyword baseline sequential, so the latency differences are descriptive rather than a controlled causal estimate. Large-company retrieval still needs a separate evaluation.
+

content.text:
The reference covers the main workspace well. These are the screens that still need dedicated designs:

- **Knowledge library:** sources for each app, customer-facing versus internal content, draft/published status, indexing failures, and updates.
- **Add/edit context:** FAQ question and answer, paste text, upload documents, import a website or GitHub document, preview extracted content, and publish or withdraw.
- **Answer testing:** ask a customer question, see Cue’s answer and cited source passages, and show when there isn’t enough context.
- **App setup:** register an app, add allowed website origins, copy the widget snippet, and configure channels and repository access.
- **Customer widget:** chat, voice, screenshots, citations, and the state where Cue needs support to help.
- **Cue customers:** Crustdata search, company results, fit reasons, shortlist/dismiss controls, and credit limits.

The landing page’s FAQ section is separate from the company FAQ manager. Most of these already have basic functional screens; they need your design treatment. I’d design **Knowledge and the customer widget first**.

content.text:
Your [cue.html](/Users/avichaldwivedi/dev/Cue/cue-demo/design/cue.html) covers **Home, Inbox, Issues and approvals, Feature requests, Growth, Agents, basic Integrations, and basic Settings**.

These still need dedicated designs:

| Missing design | What it should include |
|---|---|
| **Knowledge library** | Company sources grouped by app, customer-facing/internal visibility, draft/published status, and indexing status. |
| **FAQ and context editor** | Add/edit FAQs, paste text, upload documents, import website/GitHub content, preview extracted content, publish, and withdraw. The landing FAQ is only marketing content. |
| **Answer testing** | Ask a question, inspect Cue’s answer and cited passages, and see what happens when context is insufficient. |
| **App and connector setup** | Register an app, allowed website domains, widget installation snippet, repository/channel configuration, connection failures, and reconnect controls. The existing integration cards don’t include these configuration screens. |
| **Customer widget** | Chat, voice, screenshots, source citations, loading/failure states, and requesting human support. The operator Inbox is already designed; the customer’s widget isn’t. |
| **Crustdata customer research** | Company search, filters, results, fit reasons, company details, shortlist/dismiss, and credit usage. “Cue customers” has a tab but no dedicated contents in this file. |
| **Detailed settings** | Team members and roles, model selection, Gemini/LiteLLM usage, spending limits, and exhausted-credit states. |

For these additions, include **empty, loading, error, and permission-denied states**.

**Design Knowledge → add/edit context → test an answer first, then the customer widget.** Some already have functional screens in the app; these are the gaps in your reference design.

Your updated design is integrated with Tailwind and live in [Cue](https://cue.latchgrid.in/knowledge).

Knowledge/FAQs, answer testing and comparisons, the widget, setup, customer research, and settings now connect to real product data and actions. Gemini remains the default.

**Verified:** 345 tests passed, plus lint, type checks, production build, and desktop/mobile checks.

![Cue’s integrated UI](/Users/avichaldwivedi/dev/Cue/cue-demo/.cue/ui-knowledge-integrated.png)
<REDACTED>{"page_id":null}</REDACTED>
Okay now for all the features which i asked u, what has been implemebted and what is left?
I’ll check the current code against your requested features so I can separate what’s working, what’s only partly implemented, and what’s still pending.

The main gap is scope: FAQs, document retrieval, widget support, and the redesigned UI are working, but automatic ingestion of the whole company’s context is still pending. Cue also remains a configured company pilot; self-service onboarding and isolation between independent companies aren’t finished.

The core product flow is implemented and live in [Cue](https://cue.latchgrid.in/knowledge). **The biggest unfinished parts are automatic company-context connectors, onboarding independent companies, and unified spending controls.**

| Feature you asked for | What’s implemented | What’s left |
|---|---|---|
| **Your UI + Tailwind** | Design integrated across the dashboard, Knowledge, widget, setup, customers and settings; desktop/mobile checked. | Backend work for spending charts, alerts and invitation flows. |
| **Connect your own apps** | Register an app, configure allowed domains, copy its widget snippet and configure answers, voice and screenshots. | Broader server SDK and integrations that read or act on the app’s business data. |
| **FAQs** | Questions, approved answers, alternative questions, drafts, publishing and withdrawal. Exact matches return the approved answer. | Bulk FAQ import and automated maintenance. |
| **Add context through the UI** | Pasted text, TXT, Markdown, text-based PDF, DOCX, public webpage and public GitHub document imports; extracted-content preview. | Scanned-document OCR and additional document formats. |
| **Context retrieval** | Keyword + vector search, embeddings, versioned publication, citations, app boundaries and internal/customer visibility. | Evaluation on larger, real company knowledge bases; stronger handling of conflicting sources. |
| **Whole-company context** | Published knowledge plus Cue’s existing app/task/conversation context. | Private Notion, Drive and GitHub connectors, Slack knowledge ingestion, website crawling and automatic sync. |
| **Customer support widget** | Persistent conversations, cited answers, screenshots, recorded voice questions with spoken replies, human requests and staff replies. | Live streaming voice and deeper account-specific support actions. |
| **Answer testing** | Test questions, inspect passages/citations/tokens, compare keyword versus hybrid retrieval and different models. | Ongoing production-quality monitoring. |
| **Agents and activity** | Contextual agent conversations, saved tasks/history, role checks, approvals, supported retry/cancel and Slack thread continuity. | Custom agents and operator-agent voice. |
| **Engineering follow-through** | Approved feature specifications, repository policies, isolated Codex execution, tests, draft PRs and exact-commit review. | General bug investigation and deployment adapters across arbitrary apps. The coding worker still runs locally. |
| **Crustdata customer finding** | Real company search/enrichment, evidence, shortlist/dismiss controls, saved results and credit caps. | Contact enrichment and outreach are separate work. |
| **Team/settings** | Sign-in, configured roles, member access, workspace settings and model selection. | Invitation emails, create/join-company onboarding and full isolation between independent companies. |
| **X/Reddit/email/Slack** | X API intake, Slack and email support flows; Reddit notification intake/manual capture. | Official Reddit API discovery remains unavailable. |

Sponsor setup is also covered:

- **neatlogs:** integrated; real workflow/model traces verified.
- **Entire:** genuine shared checkpoint exists. Automatic capture still needs hooks enabled, and the latest UI build needs a fresh checkpoint/public submission snapshot.
- **cfo.ai:** business plan saved; trial cancellation verified. Organiser-issued credits remain unverified.
- **LiteLLM:** claimed and connected; original shared allocation was **$20**. Gemini remains the default. Remaining balance isn’t shown in Cue.
- **Crustdata:** account access and paid API usage verified. The advertised **5,000-credit grant** hasn’t been independently reconciled with its dashboard’s balance display.

**Other remaining work:** combined Gemini/LiteLLM spending totals, budget alerts and automatic spending pauses. Automatic issue grouping also misses some duplicates, so manual linking remains useful. Growth has verified controlled outcomes; its complete automatic positive discovery-to-review path still needs live validation.

The latest UI release passed **345 tests**, lint, type checks, production build and hosted/mobile checks. My next priority would be **automatic source connectors and sync**, followed by **company isolation/onboarding**, then **spending controls**.
Is there any more feature we should add?

I ran **two rounds with Claude using `claude -p`**. Its strongest criticism was right: my earlier plan gave Growth too little time and depended heavily on features we haven’t built.

The stronger story is:

> **Cue understands the company, helps its customers, improves its product, and finds people who can benefit from what the product actually does.**

**The standout moment should be Growth using verified product evidence.** Cue rejects an opportunity requiring an unsupported feature, then finds a suitable request, prepares a useful reply, gets exact human review, and tracks the resulting product actions.

Here’s the walkthrough I recommend:

| Time | What we show | What it proves |
|---|---|---|
| **0:00–0:08** | Open on the recorded journey: relevant X request → verified reply → Bloom visit → first memory saved → caption-search match. | Cue connects discovery to observed product use. Clearly label this **controlled traffic**. |
| **0:08–0:28** | Open company Knowledge. Show actual documents, FAQs, publication states and customer/internal visibility. Ask a question and expand its retrieved sources. | Company information is indexed and searchable; the answer has inspectable evidence. |
| **0:28–0:53** | Show the installed widget, a voice question, screenshot evidence and a cited answer. Continue into Inbox with human handoff, a staff reply and private note. | Real customer support with persistent context. |
| **0:53–1:13** | Show the recorded caption-search specification, Codex implementation, tests, exact approval and verified release. Open its agent task and Activity history. | Product improvements have evidence and accountable execution. |
| **1:13–2:08** | Give Growth **55 seconds**: source discovery, one rejected opportunity, one qualified request, supported claims, reviewed draft, verified publication and attributed product events. | Growth understands what can be recommended and follows the journey beyond generating text. |
| **2:08–2:20** | Show Crustdata company facts, fit reasons and a saved shortlist. | Cue also helps research potential business customers. Keep this distinct from acquiring Bloom users. |
| **2:20–2:50** | Show neatlogs’ actual traces, the Entire checkpoint and cfo.ai’s cost-stress scenario. | Runtime evidence, implementation history and business planning. |
| **2:50–2:58** | Return to the connected task/outcome records. | Close: **“Your company’s context, customer conversations and product work—connected through Cue.”** |

This fits the [official three-minute limit and sponsor requirements](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon).

**For “all company information indexed,” we need a precise, visible claim.** Declare the company’s required source set, then show which sources are imported, indexed, published or missing. Trace an answer back to those sources. We can demonstrate the approved corpus completely; automatic ingestion of every private company system is still unfinished.

I found one particularly valuable integration gap: **support and staff agents retrieve published knowledge, while Growth drafting currently receives verified capability claims.** Growth doesn’t yet retrieve the general company corpus or a configurable brand profile.

My recommendation on additional features:

| Priority | Addition | Smallest useful version |
|---|---|---|
| **First** | Make context coverage visible | Existing source list and tester, with an explicit required-source checklist. |
| **Second** | Give Growth supporting company evidence | Show relevant published public passages beside its verified capability claims, with source revisions recorded. |
| **Third, optional** | Consistent brand voice | Manually approved tone and example replies, applied to support and Growth drafts. |

The Growth evidence panel is roughly **3–6 engineering hours**, assuming we reuse retrieval and review infrastructure. Feeding that knowledge into generation with revision checks and meaningful validation is broader work—roughly **1.5–3 engineering days**. Those are planning estimates.

**Verified customer identity, outcome buttons and the knowledge-gaps queue remain useful product work, but they aren’t prerequisites for this demo.** A general post composer adds another story to explain.

Every major implemented feature gets coverage: source formats, model comparisons, channels, roles, task controls and setup appear in their relevant scenes or linked evidence. The deepest demonstrations are **knowledge, support and Growth**.

Before recording, the selected path must work twice, fit the runtime, and have evidence for every claimed action. A fresh automatic Growth journey needs verification; if no suitable source or budget is available, we use clearly dated retained evidence. We show observed activation without claiming organic acquisition or growth uplift.
Okay then build the context coverage, connect growth to the company knowledge, and add brand voice. Test everything, but don't make the demo video yet.

I’ll build context coverage, connect Growth to published company knowledge, and add brand voice controls. Then I’ll test the retrieval, approval and source-change paths. I’ll leave the demo video untouched.

I’m using the Convex expert skill for the backend changes. I’ll measure coverage against context the company explicitly requires, and keep brand examples separate from factual knowledge so style can’t override verified answers.

**Use both: real Cue footage for the proof, Remotion for the presentation.** I’d aim for roughly **80% product footage and 20% animation**.

Remotion can embed recorded video, so we can surround actual interactions with clean titles, zooms, captions and animated explanations. [Remotion documentation](https://www.remotion.dev/docs/html5-video)

The story should be: **“Give Cue your company’s knowledge. Watch it help customers, improve the product and support growth.”**

I’d structure it around six connected moments:

1. **Give Cue context.** Connect the app, show documents and FAQs, check Coverage, and set the brand voice. A short animation explains how the same knowledge feeds support and Growth.
2. **A customer gets help.** Ask a real question through the installed widget. Show the answer, citation and brand voice; include a short spoken interaction.
3. **A problem becomes work.** Follow a customer report into the Inbox, investigation and coding workflow. Show the patch, independent tests, exact approval and verified release. The already-fixed upload issue’s retained run should be clearly identified.
4. **The improvement becomes growth.** Show a matching customer need, the verified capability, retrieved company passages and the proposed reply. Follow the existing controlled publication through its tracked visit and activation.
5. **Cue finds its own potential customers.** Show Crustdata’s company research and reviewed shortlist. Keep this distinct from Growth promoting Bloom.
6. **Show the evidence.** Briefly connect neatlogs traces, the Entire checkpoint and cfo.ai economics to the work just shown.

**The strongest visual moment:** move from a published knowledge passage → the customer’s cited answer → a Growth draft using that same passage. That makes the shared context tangible.

To cover everything without rushing, I recommend two cuts:

- **About three minutes:** the focused submission film.
- **Six to eight minutes:** the complete product walkthrough, covering configuration, review controls and supporting features.

Remotion should make the real workflow easier to follow. The product’s actual actions and results should carry the demo.

content.text:
**Yes—Cue should support both B2B and consumer apps. I’d center Growth on helping the connected product acquire and activate customers.** Its audience could be individuals, companies or both.

Your example captures the distinction: the person using a product and the company paying for it can be different. Cue should understand both.

My initial customer hypothesis would be **small teams building software with self-service signup**, especially products used by individuals and teams. They have a natural connection between support, product improvements and growth. We still need customer evidence to validate that audience.

Growth would adapt to the product:

| Campaign | What Cue looks for | Meaningful outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Individual acquisition | Someone expressing a need the product can satisfy | They try it and complete a useful action |
| Company acquisition | A company matching the customer profile, plus evidence of a relevant need | A qualified trial, meeting or team activation |
| Existing-customer expansion | Customers whose needs fit another verified capability or plan | Adoption, upgrade or renewed use |

**Crustdata fits company acquisition.** It should research potential customers of the selected product using that product’s customer profile. Company size and industry establish potential fit; an inquiry, conversation or product action supplies stronger evidence of need. The current “Cue customers” implementation needs to become configurable and scoped to the connected app before it serves that purpose.

The competitive distinction needs care. Intercom already describes shared knowledge across support and sales, while Common Room combines product activity with account enrichment. Those vendors’ descriptions establish adjacent capabilities, rather than independently verified results. [Intercom](https://www.intercom.com/blog/announcing-fin-for-sales), [Common Room](https://www.commonroom.io/product/product-led-sales/)

**Cue’s strongest demo story is the connection between a verified product improvement and a new growth opportunity.**

I would show this sequence:

1. **Cue understands the product:** published docs, FAQs, coverage and brand voice.
2. **A customer needs help:** a cited answer, followed by a genuine problem that requires engineering work.
3. **The product improves:** investigation, patch, independent tests, human approval and verified release.
4. **Growth uses the improvement:** a relevant inquiry matches the now-supported capability; the draft shows its knowledge and verification evidence.
5. **Someone experiences value:** the reviewed recommendation leads to an actual product action, recorded in Results.
6. **Cue exercises judgment:** a second inquiry asks for an unsupported feature, and Cue keeps it as an unmet need.

The memorable moment is **the verified release making a previously unsupported recommendation eligible for review**. That demonstrates the relationship between engineering and growth.

For this submission, I recommend **keeping Bloom as the working example**, with its real evidence clearly labeled. Position Cue for consumer and B2B software; demonstrate B2B prospecting once we have a genuinely connected B2B product. Bloom currently proves the consumer journey, and generic B2B prospecting remains proposed work.

The next product step is app-specific **audience, customer profile and activation goal**, followed by rescoping Crustdata. I’d provisionally budget **1–2 focused days including tests** for that bounded pilot change. Before expanding further, compare Cue’s recommendations with a simple helpful-reply baseline on ten unseen inquiries under the same facts and model budget. Unsupported claims or increased review effort would be reasons to simplify the workflow.

The promise would become diluted if finding leads or generating marketing copy became the main story. **The engineering intervention should carry the demo; Growth should show its payoff.**

For LatchGrid, I’d build the story around this proposed scenario:

We would first establish whether that is a genuine bug, an unsupported expectation or something the documentation can resolve. Then the demo could follow:

2. **Investigate the problem:** connect the customer report to the actual failure.
3. **Make and verify the change:** show the patch, an acceptance test, approval and the deployed result.
4. **Return to the creator:** demonstrate that their original task now succeeds.
5. **Use the verified capability in Growth:** find someone expressing the same need, prepare a factual recommendation in LatchGrid’s voice, and track a real first useful action.

That final action could be **creating an output from connected research and a brief**, once we instrument and verify it. A signup alone would be weaker evidence.

The two growth audiences then make sense:

| Audience | Growth approach |
|---|---|
| Individual creators | Match expressed workflow needs to verified LatchGrid capabilities |
| Agencies | Use Crustdata to research potentially suitable businesses, then establish their actual needs before recommending LatchGrid |

Crustdata would therefore find potential **LatchGrid agency customers**, using LatchGrid’s customer profile.

Got it—just the demo story and flow. Claude’s strongest suggestion was to follow one customer problem through Cue, then show how the same company knowledge powers Growth. I’ll focus on that arc and how to cover the features without turning it into a menu tour.

**The demo should tell one connected story: Cue understands the company, helps a customer, fixes the underlying problem, and finds people the product can help.**

I discussed it with Claude. We agree the strongest moment is **the complete loop with visible proof**. I’d make it roughly four minutes, following Bloom throughout.

1. **Open with the customer’s problem — 15 seconds.**  
   We’re inside Bloom. The interface promises uploads up to 5 MB, but a 3 MB photo fails. The customer opens Cue, attaches the screenshot, and explains the problem by voice.

   Opening line: **“This customer found a bug. Watch what happens to their report.”**

2. **Reveal Cue’s understanding of the company — 35 seconds.**  
   Switch to Cue’s Inbox. Show related reports from different channels grouped into one issue.

   Open the context behind the conversation: the upload policy, relevant technical documentation, and source citations. Briefly show Knowledge’s coverage view and a brand-voice preview.

   The point the judges should grasp: **the customer-facing answer and engineering investigation use the same company knowledge, with different access to internal information.**

3. **Let the engineering agent do the work — 60 seconds.**  
   Follow the issue into Engineering. Show the actual sequence:

   **Reproduce failure → identify cause → propose code change → independent tests → human approval → deployment → deployed verification.**

   Hold briefly on the decisive evidence: the failing request, the changed limit, passing boundary tests, and the exact commit being approved. Compress long waits with an elapsed-time caption.

   The dramatic moment is **“Verified” appearing after deployment**, followed by the original upload succeeding in Bloom.

4. **Close the customer loop and show how Cue learns — 35 seconds.**  
   Return to the same conversation. The customer receives the update in Bloom’s voice and selects **Solved**.

   Then show one unanswered question from the knowledge-gaps queue: open its original conversation, add a verified answer, publish it, and ask it again through the widget.

   **The second customer gets the answer immediately.** That makes knowledge management feel useful rather than administrative.

5. **Show customers shaping the roadmap — 20 seconds.**  
   Open a grouped feature request. Show how many people asked, their original messages, Cue’s proposed specification, and the human decision.

   Keep this short: it demonstrates that Cue can distinguish a bug, a missing answer, and a feature request—and handle each appropriately.

6. **Make Growth the second payoff — 55 seconds.**  
   Show a public post from someone looking for a capability Bloom actually supports.

   Cue connects their need to company knowledge and verified product evidence, then drafts a useful reply in Bloom’s voice. Open the evidence behind the recommendation. Briefly show a request Bloom cannot satisfy being routed to Requests.

   Follow a reviewed reply into its tracked journey: **reply → visit → first meaningful action in Bloom**. Any earlier controlled activation should be identified clearly.

   Closing product line: **“Cue uses what your company knows to help existing customers—and help the right new customers discover you.”**

7. **Finish with proof — 20 seconds.**  
   Show the relevant neatlogs trace, the Entire checkpoint, and the cfo.ai business plan. Tie each to its purpose: understanding failures, preserving engineering decisions, and checking the business economics.

Use real product footage as the main visual. Small captions and zooms can guide attention. Setup, connections, and model selection can appear as brief inserts beside the actions they enable.

**The two moments to build the film around are the original upload succeeding and a customer question becoming reusable company knowledge. Growth then shows that this same context has value beyond support.**
